title: Strongly coupled ultracompressed self-cavity plasmon polaritons at millikelvin temperatures
authors: Luojia Zhang, Andrew T. Pierce, Xuepeng Wang, Simon Reinhardt, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Kin Fai Mak, Jie Shan, Debanjan Chowdhury, Valla Fatemi
abstract: Van der Waals heterostructures exhibit self-cavity resonances from sub-terahertz to terahertz frequencies and thus offer an attractive route toward realizing cavity-modified phases of matter. Spectroscopy of such systems calls for high frequency resolution at millikelvin temperatures, which is extremely challenging with existing methods. Here we demonstrate a new platform for realizing and probing such systems. Superconducting layers define self-cavity structures with electromagnetic volume compression of order $10^7$. With an integrated graphene layer, we observe underdamped cavity plasmon polaritons at frequencies as low as 0.04 THz and which exhibit avoided crossings with cavity modes. To measure such spectra, we deploy a millikelvin-compatible sub-THz spectrometer based on a superconducting circuit. This work paves the way for simultaneous spectroscopy and transport measurements of cavity-matter hybrid systems at millikelvin temperatures.
summary: The research introduces a novel, superconducting-based spectrometer to probe plasmonic cavities formed in Van der Waals heterostructures at millikelvin temperatures. By coupling a superconducting cavity mode with a graphene-derived plasmon mode, the authors successfully demonstrated strong light-matter coupling. This platform enables simultaneous spectroscopy and transport measurements crucial for advancing cavity quantum matter research.
main_problem: The challenge is realizing and spectroscopically probing cavity-modified phases of matter in Van der Waals heterostructures at extremely low temperatures and sub-THz frequencies.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated a platform using superconducting circuits and graphene to observe underdamped cavity plasmon polaritons and evidence of strong light-matter coupling via avoided crossings.
method: The measurement relies on a novel, millikelvin-compatible sub-THz spectrometer based on Josephson junctions, which acts as both the emitter and detector of the sub-THz radiation.
model_or_system: The physical system involves Van der Waals heterostructures, specifically superconducting layers forming a Kinetic Inductance Broadside Cavity (KIBC) coupled to an integrated graphene layer, forming a tunable hybrid plasmonic system.
key_observables: Underdamped cavity plasmon polariton frequencies, avoided crossings between cavity and matter modes, and the DC junction current ($I_{DC}$) measured via Josephson spectroscopy.
important_parameters: Millikelvin temperatures ($T \approx 10 	ext{ mK}$), sub-THz frequencies (down to 0.04 THz), and electromagnetic volume compression of order $10^7$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on an effective circuit model and Random Phase Approximation (RPA) calculations for graphene's response.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic of the Josephson spectrometer coupled to the KIBC, the measured $I-V$ characteristics, and the impedance spectra showing mode resonances for both KIBC and graphene-coupled structures.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the need for the platform, details the superconducting circuit and graphene integration, presents the measurement methodology using Josephson spectroscopy, and finally reports the observation of coupled plasmon modes.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges cavity Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) principles with solid-state 2D materials physics, providing a highly controllable, low-loss platform for studying light-matter interaction in engineered quantum systems at cryogenic temperatures.

The KIBC is defined by high-KI superconductors separated by dielectric layers. Low-dimensional quantum materials can be sandwiched between the two layers. The cavity is connected to a Josephson junction that acts as an emitter and detector of sub-THz photons, allowing for measurement of the high-frequency electrodynamic response of the KIBC. An insulating Si substrate hosts an aluminum Josephson junction connected to Nb electrodes, which are in turn connected to a lossy Pt transmission line. The Pt transmission line is wire bonded to an on-chip voltage divider on a second, separate Si substrate (see Supplementary Information). The voltages Vsense and VJJ are probed by measuring across the Pt transmission line electrodes, and the DC junction current is given by Vsense/Rbias. (b) Side view of the NbN/hBN bilayer KIBC.
